The Christian epitaphs of the 3rd–8th centuries almost never name the occupation of the deceased: with the same lexicon and the same rules we found an occupational title in 0.3% of the texts, against 5.5% in the mostly earlier, non-Christian inscriptions of EDR. The difference does not come only from the shorter Christian texts: among texts of at least 40 letters it is still 0.7% against 6.8%. All 115 hits in the Christian inscriptions were read one by one, and 23 false or uncertain hits were left out (for example “mensorum”, here a corrupt form of “months”, not a surveyor). The most frequent: nurse (11), shorthand writer (9), chamberlain (7), physician (5), faber (smith, craftsman) (4), banker, money-changer (4). The Greek texts are not covered by this Latin lexicon.
